description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
Firstly, we trained 21 members of the cooperative and the Sounbouyadi group (of which 18 female) on: - tomato & pepper cultivation, Good Agricultural practices, Climate Smart agriculture, etc. - practical skills for tomato & pepper cultivation - lead farmer approach - entrepreneurship - bookkeeping and critical reflection on actions to improve the performance of the trainings to be given These topics were part of the original training plan. What we did differently is the focus from partly theoretical/partly practical to fully practical training as most participants were illiterate. Bookkeeping was therefore difficult, but we focused here on record keeping mainly. We established in the end two times a training field. The first one (established during the first training) did not succeed because both the soil and the water were way too acid (pH of about 4.5). The pH meter was not brought to the cooperative at that time. The second training field was established during the third training week on another location. This crops (tomato, pepper, eggplant) didn’t survive the nursery stage due to a problem with the water supply. Now a new crop is in the nursery and ready for planting. Training on the next stages was provided throughout the project. Of course we could work for the practical training in the field with the crops that the farmers were growing there already. Although not successful, the participants did learn a lot about setting up a crop, what they need to consider and what can go wrong.
Two demonstration days were held with the participants to spread the newly gained skills and knowledge to a broader group, for the members of the Groupe de Yeniyah (22 persons). Instead of inviting people, we went to new fields people who were interested to learn. This was done during two days. The outreach of these groups was significant, as they indicated that the knowledge spread by them reached about 300 women in the region. We did not reach a yield increase of at least 30% for tomato and pepper growing at the demo plots. As said above, the tomato and pepper (and eggplant) crops didn’t survive the nursery stage two times due to challenges with soil, water and management. The coming crop could still reach this, but is outside of the project period.
